clue.text: Though responsible for many a stick-up, he's no footpad

definitions.text: Though responsible for many a stick-up, he's no footpad

parts.words: Though responsible for many a stick-up, he's no footpad
parts.note: a stick-up reads as a hold-up by a robber, but here it is a notice pasted on a wall; a footpad is a highway robber on foot

explanation.surface: A man behind countless hold-ups who is somehow not a robber at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick-up' sounds like armed robbery, which the mention of a footpad (an old word for a robber on foot) reinforces; the man actually sticks posters up on walls.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who pastes up posters and notices responsible for many items stuck to walls.

clue.text: Raven's perch

parts.note: in Poe's poem The Raven the bird sits on a sculpted head of Pallas above the door

explanation.surface: Where a large black bird sits.
explanation.walkthrough: In Poe's The Raven the bird perches 'upon a bust of Pallas just above my chamber door'.
explanation.definitionFit: A sculpted head and shoulders, as of Pallas in Poe's poem, where the bird sat.

clue.text: Face up to being prostrated

parts.note: face up reads as confronting something, but describes a body put down on its back

explanation.surface: Bravely accepting being knocked flat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Face up to' looks like 'confront'; read literally, someone stretched out face up has been put down flat.
explanation.definitionFit: Put down flat, as a body laid out lying on its back.

clue.text: Minor blasts of advertising ?

definitions.meaning: small gusts of wind or breath

explanation.surface: Small bursts of promotional copy.
explanation.definitionFit: Small gusts of breath or air; also inflated commendations of a product or book.

clue.text: The cheese presumably is rather high !

definitions.text: The cheese presumably is rather high !

parts.words: The cheese presumably is rather high !
parts.note: high reads as smelly and ripe, but the cheese's name splits as if standing on tall poles

explanation.surface: A ripe cheese smelling strongly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High' suggests a strong smell; the cheese's name splits as STILT ON, raised up on stilts.
explanation.definitionFit: A strong blue-veined English cheese, whose name looks like being up on stilts.

clue.text: Puts forth one's best efforts ?

parts.note: straining oneself to the utmost, and also stretching or holding something out

explanation.surface: Someone trying as hard as they can.
explanation.walkthrough: To try one's hardest is to stretch oneself fully; 'puts forth' also means holds out, as an arm.
explanation.definitionFit: Stretches out or offers; also exerts oneself to the full.

clue.text: Army shot to pieces

indicators.note: something shot to pieces is broken up, so the letters of the preceding word are rearranged

explanation.surface: A military force blown apart in battle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to pieces' rearranges SHOT.
explanation.definitionFit: A host is an old word for a great multitude, especially an army, as in the heavenly host.

clue.text: Akimbo ? Poor show !

definitions.meaning: arms akimbo means hands on hips with the joints of the arms jutting outward
shabby, with clothes worn through at the joint of the sleeve

explanation.surface: Disapproving of someone standing with hands on hips.
explanation.walkthrough: Arms akimbo push the joints of the arms outward; the phrase also means shabby, sleeves worn through.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally with arms jutting sideways; idiomatically shabby and threadbare.

clue.text: Oily agent of pure intent

indicators.note: oily suggests something slippery and shifting, so the letters slide into a new order

explanation.surface: Something greasy that sounds well-meaning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oily' rearranges PURE INTENT; the answer is a solvent, so the oily image doubles as a hint.
explanation.definitionFit: Turpentine is a solvent used to thin paint, an agent for dissolving.

clue.text: Are they one up on cheese-parers ?

definitions.text: Are they one up on cheese-parers ?

parts.words: Are they one up on cheese-parers ?
parts.note: a cheese-parer is a miser who pares the rind off cheese; someone who would skin a flint is meaner still

explanation.surface: Asking whether one group of misers outdoes another.
explanation.walkthrough: A cheese-parer is a penny-pincher; the answer's misers are imagined skinning flints, a harder and stingier job than paring cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: Misers or tightwads, people so mean they would try to skin a flint stone.

clue.text: It is the -to every wandering bark " (Shakespeare)

definitions.text: It is the -to every wandering bark " (Shakespeare)

parts.words: It is the -to every wandering bark " (Shakespeare)
parts.note: a gap-fill quotation from Shakespeare's Sonnet 116, where love is the fixed guiding light for every lost ship

explanation.surface: A line of Shakespeare with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Sonnet 116 says love 'is the star to every wandering bark', a bark being a sailing ship steered by the stars.
explanation.definitionFit: In Sonnet 116 love is the guiding celestial light by which every lost ship navigates.

clue.text: Decree confounds 17

indicators.note: to confound is to throw into confusion, so the letters of the other entry are mixed up

parts.note: the solution to 17 down

explanation.surface: An official ruling that baffles somebody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confounds' rearranges the answer to 17 down.
explanation.definitionFit: To ordain is to order or establish by authority.

clue.text: Lucy has not changed, or has she ?

indicators.note: the letters of the preceding two words are altered into a new order

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a woman called Lucy has altered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changed' rearranges HAS NOT. Lucy Ashton is the heroine of Walter Scott's novel The Bride of Lammermoor.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucy Ashton is the doomed heroine of Scott's The Bride of Lammermoor, the source of Donizetti's opera Lucia.

clue.text: Milton shows some preference for the primrose

indicators.note: only some of the word is used, so its final letter is dropped

parts.note: rather expresses preference, as in 'I would rather'

explanation.surface: A remark that the poet Milton favoured primroses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some' cuts the last letter from RATHER. Milton wrote of 'the rathe primrose' in Lycidas, rathe meaning early-blooming.
explanation.definitionFit: Milton's epithet in Lycidas, an old word meaning early, used of the flower that blooms first in spring.

clue.text: Superfluous, advice to the miniskirt maker ?

definitions.text: Superfluous, advice to the miniskirt maker ?

parts.words: Superfluous, advice to the miniskirt maker ?
parts.note: telling a maker of miniskirts to make things shorter is unnecessary, since they are already short

explanation.surface: Pointless tips for a designer of short skirts.
explanation.walkthrough: Telling a miniskirt maker to shorten things is superfluous advice: the skirts are short already.
explanation.definitionFit: To shorten, especially a word or text.

clue.text: Swear words must be put in writing

definitions.text: Swear words must be put in writing

parts.words: Swear words must be put in writing
parts.note: swear words reads as oaths of bad language, but means statements made under oath and written down

explanation.surface: A rule that profanity be written down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swear words' suggests profanity; it means sworn statements, which are made in writing.
explanation.definitionFit: Written statements confirmed by oath, for use as legal evidence.

clue.text: A bare skin has nothing on a clown

parts.note: to be in the buff is to be naked, so bare skin is buff
O looks like zero, nothing
taken as written

explanation.surface: A naked person is less than a clown in some sense.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests nudity outdoing a clown; in fact BUFF, O and ON are simply placed in a row.
explanation.definitionFit: A buffoon is a jester or comic fool.

clue.text: No use asking her for a match !

definitions.text: No use asking her for a match !

parts.words: No use asking her for a match !
parts.note: the seventeenth-century poet Katherine Philips was called matchless, so she has no match to give

explanation.surface: A woman who never has a light for a cigarette.
explanation.walkthrough: Katherine Philips, the 17th-century poet, wrote as Orinda and was praised as 'the matchless Orinda'.
explanation.definitionFit: The pen name of the poet Katherine Philips, known as 'the matchless' one.

clue.text: It's grown on the estate of Tennyson's Lady, we hear

indicators.note: signals that the word is identified by its pronunciation rather than its spelling

parts.note: Tennyson's poem The Lady of Shalott names her home Shalott

explanation.surface: Something cultivated on the land of the woman in Tennyson's poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we hear' signals that SHALOTT, from Tennyson's poem The Lady of Shalott, sounds like the onion.
explanation.definitionFit: A small onion-like bulb raised as a vegetable crop.

clue.text: Being abusive from the right not so good

parts.note: ailing means unwell, not feeling so good

explanation.surface: Someone hurling insults from a right-wing position, not a nice thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from the right' tempts a political reading; it simply gives R.
explanation.definitionFit: To rail is to complain bitterly or scold, so railing means scolding abusively.

clue.text: Victim of a youthful lapidator

parts.note: a lapidator is one who stones; the youthful stoner is the boy David

explanation.surface: Someone stoned by a young person.
explanation.walkthrough: A lapidator throws stones; the young David killed the Philistine giant with a stone from his sling.
explanation.definitionFit: The Philistine giant slain by the boy David with a slingshot stone.

clue.text: Time for a drink in Africa

definitions.text: Time for a drink in Africa

parts.words: Time for a drink in Africa
parts.note: in colonial Africa the evening drink was the ..., taken at a particular hour

explanation.surface: Wondering when one may have a drink in Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'sundowner' is the drink taken in colonial Africa at evening, when the sun sets.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunset, the hour at which the African sundowner drink is taken.

clue.text: Enveloped in self-importance ?

parts.note: describes a conceited person and also a sealed envelope fastened shut

explanation.surface: Someone wrapped up in their own grandeur.
explanation.walkthrough: An envelope is stuck up when sealed; a snob is stuck-up too.
explanation.definitionFit: Snobbishly conceited; also, literally, sealed down like an envelope.

clue.text: What singular food !

parts.note: singular reads as strange, but means grammatically single: the word for food is usually used in the plural

explanation.surface: An exclamation at some odd dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singular' looks like 'peculiar' but points to grammar: the word for victuals is normally plural, so its singular form is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An article of food, the rarely used singular of viands, provisions.

clue.text: The waters of Slough

indicators.note: of here means made out of, so the town's name supplies the letters with its opening letter carried round to the end

explanation.surface: The rivers and ponds of the English town of Slough.
explanation.walkthrough: Slough is a town west of London; 'of' derives the answer from it by carrying its first letter to the end. There is no other device, so the definition sits beside a bare letter shift.
explanation.definitionFit: Irish lakes or sea inlets, the Irish counterpart of Scottish lochs.

clue.text: Dyer's Weed, but not strictly botanically

definitions.text: Dyer's Weed, but not strictly botanically

parts.words: Dyer's Weed, but not strictly botanically
parts.note: a plant used by dyers, though not the species botanists name dyer's weed

explanation.surface: A dye plant described with botanical caution.
explanation.walkthrough: Botanists reserve 'dyer's weed' for weld; this reddish dye shrub is a dyer's plant only in a loose sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A shrub whose leaves give a reddish-brown dye for hair and skin.

clue.text: Gooseberry might well be made one of !

definitions.text: Gooseberry might well be made one of !

parts.words: Gooseberry might well be made one of !
parts.note: playing gooseberry, the unwanted third, makes one look silly; also a fruit pudding of cream and purée

explanation.surface: The third wheel on a date being made to look silly.
explanation.walkthrough: To play gooseberry is to be the unwanted third person; gooseberries are also made into a creamy pudding of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: A silly person, and a dessert of puréed fruit folded into cream.

clue.text: Avoid that barrack-square order

definitions.meaning: the drill command 'Attention!' is barked as a clipped short form

explanation.surface: Keep clear of that shouted command on the parade ground.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep away from; also the clipped drill-sergeant form of the command 'Attention!'.

clue.text: Bill is a legendary lover

parts.note: AC, short for account, is a bill
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man called Bill is a romantic figure of legend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a name; it is an account, AC.
explanation.definitionFit: Acis was the shepherd beloved of the nymph Galatea in Greek myth.

clue.text: Scot defying the weather ?

parts.note: a Scottish surname that is also the name of a waterproof coat

explanation.surface: A hardy Scotsman braving the elements.
explanation.walkthrough: The surname is Scottish, and Charles Macintosh gave his name to the rubberised raincoat.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a Scottish clan surname and a waterproof raincoat.

clue.text: " All zeal all zeal, Mr. -" (Marryat)

parts.note: a gap-fill quotation from Captain Marryat's novel about a young naval midshipman

explanation.surface: A quotation from Marryat with the name missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Frederick Marryat's novel is Mr Midshipman Easy; the captain's refrain to the hero is 'All zeal, Mr Easy'.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of the hero of Marryat's novel Mr Midshipman Easy.

clue.text: Dejected, naturally, with one man down

parts.note: a chap is a man
fallen means knocked down

explanation.surface: A team feeling low after losing a player.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with one man down' sounds like a sports team short-handed; it is simply CHAP followed by FALLEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Chapfallen means with jaw hanging, downcast and dispirited.
